summary:
Article 120 of Uzbekistan's 1994 Criminal Code criminalises consensual sexual conduct between men and carries a maximum penalty of three years' imprisonment. Human Dignity Trust, Human Rights Watch's World Report 2024 and the UK Home Office's country-policy note of July 2024 all record the offence as in force. The Home Office documents prosecutions under Article 120 between 2009 and 2023, so the provision is applied rather than dormant.

Uzbekistan has no legal gender recognition. A trans visitor remains, in law, the sex assigned at birth, and Human Dignity Trust notes that transgender people may be prosecuted under Article 120 on that basis. Human Rights Watch reports that police target gay and bisexual men and trans women with arbitrary detention, prosecution and imprisonment.

Forced examinations of detainees amount to torture, according to the World Health Organization's assessment cited by Human Rights Watch, and impunity for police ill-treatment persists. The US State Department's 2021 human rights report records torture, ill-treatment and arbitrary detention in custody alongside social stigma and violence against LGBT people.

The State Department's 2023 report records LGBTQI+ people arrested and then released, or threatened with arrest, unless they paid bribes, and police coercing LGBTQI+ people to inform on others under threat of prison. Human Rights Watch's March 2021 reporting describes gay and bisexual men facing discrimination, violence, blackmail and extortion from both state and non-state actors with almost no protection available.

LGBTI organisations cannot register in Uzbekistan and operate unofficially, so formally recognised advocacy, legal aid and support structures do not exist. The Home Office note records that rural social taboo drives discrimination, and the State Department's 2023 report records continued societal harassment alongside self-censorship by websites and bloggers covering LGBTQI+ issues.

In November 2024 Alisher Qodirov, leader of the Milliy Tiklanish party, announced he was drafting a law to ban discussion of LGBTQ people. In April 2023 the Constitution was amended leaving "sexual orientation" out of its enumerated protected categories while listing gender, race, religion and nationality.

ECOM's 2024 national report on violations of LGBT people's rights in Uzbekistan addresses the legislative framework, anti-discrimination provisions, the criminalisation of HIV transmission, legal gender recognition, access to human rights, and the rights to health and to work.
tangentialFactors:
Human Rights Watch urged decriminalisation in March 2021, at a time when Uzbekistan held a seat on the UN Human Rights Council.

Adjacent legal exposure extends beyond Article 120: ECOM's 2024 report covers the criminalisation of HIV transmission as a distinct issue in Uzbek law.

The draft law announced in November 2024 was presented by its sponsor as inspired by foreign political commentary about "LGBT propaganda" in schools.
localsOnly:
LGBTI organisations in Uzbekistan cannot obtain registration and operate unofficially, which leaves residents without formally recognised advocacy, legal aid or support structures.

Rural social taboo drives discrimination against LGBT people, and the State Department's 2023 report records continued societal harassment alongside self-censorship by websites and bloggers covering LGBTQI+ issues.

Police have coerced LGBTQI+ people into informing on others under threat of prison, and residents arrested have been released or had charges dropped only after paying bribes.

Uzbek law provides no legal gender recognition, so residents cannot change the sex or name recorded in identity documents to match their lived gender.

ECOM's 2024 report covers access to health and to work, and the criminalisation of HIV transmission, among the areas it examines.
outOfScopeNotes:
Article 120's text addresses conduct between men. How it is applied to a trans woman, a trans man, or a foreign national is not documented in the sources reviewed, and no case involving a visitor appears among them.

No sourced information was identified on entry and visa rules, document-marker or passport-gender policy for trans travellers, border screening practice, or bathroom and facilities law in Uzbekistan.

The status of the draft law announced in November 2024 is unresolved: the sources record the announcement, not enactment or parliamentary progress.

Enforcement data is unevenly dated. The Home Office case record runs to 2023, Human Rights Watch's World Report covers 2023, the State Department material covers 2021 and 2023, and ECOM's report covers 2024. No per-capita or case-count data on Article 120 prosecutions is provided.

Wikipedia is the only source among those reviewed for the November 2024 draft law and the April 2023 constitutional enumeration; both rest on a single source and were not corroborated by the other material.
